Why lighthouses blink in patterns

By A. Keeper

Every lighthouse along a coast has its own rhythm of light and darkness. Sailors call this rhythm the characteristic, and it lets a navigator tell one tower from another at night, when the buildings themselves cannot be seen at all.

A light might show a single flash every five seconds, two quick flashes followed by a long pause, or a steady beam that is briefly eclipsed. These patterns are printed on nautical charts, so that a sailor who counts the seconds between flashes can find the matching tower on the map and work out where the ship is.

How the patterns are made

Early lighthouses used clockwork to turn a set of lenses around a lamp. Each panel of glass gathered the light into a beam, and the number and spacing of the panels decided how often the beam swept past the watcher. Modern lights often use electronic flashers instead, but the published characteristic stays the same so that old charts remain useful for a long time.

  • Fixed: a steady light that never goes out.
  • Flashing: the light is on for less time than it is off.
  • Occulting: the light is on for longer than it is off.
